lines: Watch the same program run twice: once on a single core, once spread across sixteen, and the second run finishes in a fraction of the time.
Now run a different program of exactly the same size, written as one long dependent chain, and adding cores buys it nothing at all.
Before the reveal, think about what a tree of additions actually forces: how deep is its longest unavoidable chain, and does that depth change if you hand it more workers?
answer: The longest chain here is only four additions deep, so unlimited workers finish in four steps — but that same four-deep chain is also the hard ceiling on how much speed-up any worker count can ever buy.

lines: Give a name to what just happened: the total number of additions is the work, the longest unavoidable chain is the span, and dividing one by the other tells you the most speed-up physically available.
Neither number depends on how many workers you actually have — they are properties of the dependency structure itself, fixed before a single worker is assigned.
Take the identical set of additions and force them into one strict order instead of a tree, and the span stops being four and becomes the entire count of additions.
Not one operation changed — only the order they are permitted to run in — and that alone erased every bit of available parallelism.
A divide-and-conquer algorithm whose two halves run side by side only pays for the slower of those halves, plus whatever work has to happen afterward to combine them.
A merge sort built this way inherits its span almost entirely from that final combining step, because the two halves it waits on finish together, not one after another.
Double the size of the input and watch what each of the two numbers does: one grows in a straight line, the other grows faster than that.
Because one outpaces the other, the ratio between them — the available parallelism — keeps climbing as the problem gets bigger, which is exactly backward from what a fixed ceiling would predict.

Two separate limits apply here, and neither one is a guess: workers can never finish faster than the work divided evenly among them, and no worker count, however large, can ever beat the span by itself.
Those two floors hold independently of any scheduling decision — they are consequences of the dependency structure, not of how well a scheduler happens to be built.
A schedule that refuses to ever leave a worker idle while some ready task is waiting turns out to have a provable ceiling of its own: work divided by workers, plus the span.
That guarantee is not close to optimal by luck — it can be shown to land within a factor of two of whatever the best possible schedule could achieve, for any number of workers at all.

Running that exact never-idle rule on the same tree of additions, across one worker, a handful, and many, produces step counts that sit right where the two floors and this new ceiling predict they should.
Past a certain worker count the measured steps simply stop falling, because the span itself has already become the only thing left to wait on.
Now take away the one assumption that made the previous scheduler simple: a single list that every worker checks before deciding what to run next.
Ask what an individual worker, holding only its own private list, should actually do the moment that list runs dry.
answer: Reach out to some other worker, chosen with no favoritism at all, and take a piece of its remaining work — a coordinator was never required in the first place.

lines: Each worker treats its own list the way a single-threaded program treats its own call stack, taking from one particular end while it has anything left to do.

An idle worker becomes a thief instead, reaching into some other worker's list from the opposite end — deliberately the oldest entry there, the one statistically most likely to still be carrying real work underneath it.

This protocol only carries a guarantee for a particular shape of computation — one where every dependency returns straight back to whichever task created it, the shape an ordinary recursive split-and-combine program already has.

For exactly that shape, the expected running time comes out to work divided by workers, plus a constant times the span — the identical guarantee as before, now achieved with nobody coordinating anything centrally.

Running this stealing protocol through a step-by-step simulation on a much larger version of the same tree shows a single worker completing everything alone, since there is nobody around to steal from.
Add more workers and the share of the work that changes hands through a steal does rise, but even with a great many workers involved, that stolen share stays a comfortably small slice of the total.

This is not a hypothetical scheduler: it is the one a specific research language was built around from the start, and its own modern successor still advertises tuning its scheduling to whatever machine it happens to run on.
A popular Rust library runs this identical protocol under a familiar-sounding call, right down to warning that letting one half wait on the other inside it can cause an outright deadlock.

A different, widely used asynchronous runtime steals from private queues too, but for tasks that spend their time waiting on networks and disks rather than pure dependent computation — a related idea, applied somewhere this topic's guarantee does not reach.
One detail was deliberately set aside: the moment a worker and a thief both reach for the very last entry in a list at the same instant.

That particular race has a well-known, carefully engineered fix elsewhere in this course — naming the problem honestly here does not require building its solution before this topic's own guarantee can stand.
Work, span and their ratio set a hard ceiling on one machine's many cores, and this stealing protocol reaches that ceiling without any central coordination at all.
The next question drops the assumption this whole topic quietly made: that every core can still read the same memory for free, no matter how many machines are actually involved.
